title: Epistolae
author: Braulio Caesaraugustiani Episcopus
source: Translated by Claude from tmp1394.tmp1394.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Et ideo si quid in hoc displicuerit, sibi imputet quae tantum amat, ut timorem tollat. Nam perfecta charitas foras mittit timorem. Speciali quo- que gratia fretus speciali domino, in quo vires san- ctae Ecclesiae consistunt, suggero ut quia Eusebius noster metropolitanus decessit, habeas misericordiae curam. Et hoc filio tuo, nostro domino suggeras ut utilem illi loco praeficiat, cujus doctrina et sanctitas caeteris sit vitae forma. Hunc autem filium praesen- tem beatissimae potestati vestrae per omnia commen- do, ut tam de his quae hic suggessimus, quam etiam de his quae supra questi sumus, eloquio vestro per eum illustrari mereamur.
passages.english: And so, if anything in this has displeased [you], let her who loves so much that she takes away fear lay it to her own account. For perfect charity casts out fear. Relying also on special grace from a special lady, in whom the strength of the holy Church rests, I suggest that, since our metropolitan Eusebius has died, you take care to show mercy. And suggest this to your son, our lord, that he set over that see a useful man, whose teaching and holiness may be a pattern of life for the rest. I commend this son, who is present, to your most blessed power in all things, so that, both concerning what we have suggested here and concerning what we complained of above, we may deserve to be enlightened by your words through him.
passages.notes: 'Speciali domino' is read as addressed to a lady (feminine context: 'quae tantum amat', 'filio tuo'); the Latin form domino may stand for dominae or the addressee may be male. 'Habeas misericordiae curam' is rendered loosely; the sense of the request is not wholly clear.

passages.original: devotionem enim tuam eo quam maxime approbo, quo etiam importunitatem tuam nec ibi cohibes ad sancti studii exercitationem ampliandam, ubi manet tibi scientia parum posse invenire quae- sita : nam cum quotidie in lege Domini mediteris, et beatissimorum Patrum peritissimorumque revol- vas paginas virorum, quid in nobis, aut quantulum est, quod aut ipse velis addiscere, aut de quibus contingat tibi sacrum desiderium alere? Sufficit, et valde sufficit, ut amicum tuum legas sanctum Augu- stinum, ut Hieronymum, ut Hilarium, ut caeteros doctissimos viros, quos et mihi commemorare lon- gum est et te usui habere dubium non est. Eorum te sermo pascat, eorum sententiae instruant, imo isti cuncta quae quaeris perdoceant, eisque contentus nostram paupertatulam nec in propatulo trahas, nec invidentium oculis nudam videndamque exponas.
passages.english: For I approve your devotion all the more, in that you do not restrain your importunity in enlarging the exercise of holy study even where knowledge remains to you that you can find little of what you seek. For since you meditate daily on the law of the Lord, and turn over the pages of the most blessed Fathers and most learned men, what is in us, or how little is it, that you should either wish to learn yourself, or by which you might happen to nourish your holy desire? It is enough, and more than enough, that you read your friend Saint Augustine, Jerome, Hilary, and the other most learned men, whom it would take me long to list and whom you doubtless have in use. Let their discourse feed you, let their judgements instruct you, indeed let them teach you thoroughly all that you seek; and, content with them, do not drag our little poverty out into the open, nor expose it naked and to be gazed at before the eyes of the envious.

passages.original: imo illud Virgilianum a : Nam paradigma tuum illud in armatura compositum quam mihi erat pervium et pede, ut aiunt, conte- rere, excepto illud pace Gregorii quod peculatum imo corruptum vidi. Sed dum studemus et charitati servire, et te non amittere, omittimus cuncta, nec aliquod risu dignum inserimus, ne habeat ingratos fabula nostra jocos, secundum Ovidium, ac secun- dum Appium caninam videamur exercere facundiam : sed ut dixi, spretis his, officii nostri functionem exse- quentes, et Magistri Domini Christi humilitatem te- nentes, magis volumus sequi cum qui ait : Dorsum meum posui ad flagella, et maxillas meas ad palmas.
passages.english: or rather that saying of Virgil: for that model of yours composed in armour, how easy it was for me to trample it, as they say, even with my foot, except for that [part], by Gregory's leave, which I saw was embezzled, or rather corrupted. But while we strive both to serve charity and not to lose you, we pass over everything, and insert nothing worthy of laughter, lest our tale have unwelcome jokes, according to Ovid, and lest, according to Appius, we seem to practise a dog's eloquence. But, as I said, scorning these things, carrying out the duty of our office and holding to the humility of our Master the Lord Christ, we would rather follow him who says: I gave my back to the scourges and my cheeks to the blows.
passages.notes: The opening is fragmentary and the text appears corrupt: the Virgil quotation is missing (marked by a footnote 'a'), and 'in armatura compositum', 'excepto illud pace Gregorii quod peculatum' are uncertain in sense. 'Pede conterere' rendered 'trample with my foot'. 'Canina facundia' is attributed to Appius (Appius Claudius).

passages.original: Ego autem non solum injuriis tuis non moveor, sed blande quae scripsisti recipio, et tibi, si quod offendi, veniam peto, ac ut me magis magisque diligas, opto, memor quia Christiani sumus, et dispendia anima- rum nostrarum pertimescere non amare debemus. Ecce si ante tibi fuit motus, modo sit modus : et cui potius placent vina quam verba, caveat vina, ne cum offendant verba. En dum urceum fingere volo, ut ait Terentius, amphoram finxit manus. Nam brevem schedulam scribere cogitaveram sed pene prolixa evasit epistola; tu vero pro epistola testamentum direxisti, quod forte nisi post mortem tuam firmetur, nam modo legitime resera- tum non est.
passages.english: But I am not only unmoved by your insults, but receive kindly what you wrote, and ask your pardon if I have offended in anything, and I desire that you love me more and more, mindful that we are Christians and ought to fear, not love, the losses of our souls. See, if there was agitation in you before, let there now be a limit; and let him who likes wine better than words beware of wine, lest words then offend. Look: while I mean to shape a pitcher, as Terence says, my hand has shaped a wine-jar. For I had thought to write a short note, but it has turned out almost a lengthy letter; you, however, sent a testament instead of a letter, which perhaps will not be confirmed except after your death, for it has not yet been lawfully unsealed.
passages.notes: The pitcher/amphora saying is from Horace (Ars Poetica), not Terence; the attribution is the author's. 'Cum offendant' probably for 'tum offendant'.

passages.original: Age, piissime domine, ut vestra pro hoc merces clareat ante Dominum. Septem Collationes, quas memoratus Cassianus Joviniano, Minervio, Leontio, et Theodoro scripsit, jam hic Christianis tribuenti- bus, habemus. Reliquas decem, quas Helladio et Leontio episcopis, et alias septem, quas sancto Ho- norato atque Eucherio se asserit edidisse, minime habemus, Ilas exoramus ut percipere vobis largien- tibus mereamur.
passages.english: Act, most dutiful lord, so that your reward for this may shine before the Lord. The seven Conferences which the aforementioned Cassian wrote to Jovinian, Minervius, Leontius and Theodore we already have here, through the gift of Christians. The remaining ten, which he says he published for the bishops Helladius and Leontius, and the other seven for Saint Honoratus and Eucherius, we do not have at all; we beg that by your bounty we may deserve to receive them.

passages.original: Nam in quibusdam etiam Codicibus Graecis tribus et uno Latino, et uno etiam Syro inter se consentientibus inventus est Mathusa- lam sex annis ante diluvium fuisse defunctus. Haec sanctus Augustinus per intervalla, ita ut posuimus, sicut et beatus Hieronymus narrat.
passages.english: For in certain manuscripts also, three Greek, one Latin and also one Syriac, agreeing with one another, Methuselah was found to have died six years before the Flood. Saint Augustine [says] these things at intervals, just as we have set them down, as blessed Jerome also relates.
passages.notes: The last sentence is elliptical; the verb 'says' is supplied.
